title: Auxiliary verbs (have/do/can etc.); I think so / I hope so etc.
subtitle: Yes, I have. / So am I. / I hope so.
summary: Use auxiliary verbs (have, do, can, was etc.) on their own to avoid repeating words, and use I think so / I hope not etc. as short answers.

lesson.heading: Auxiliary verb + main verb
rows: The hotel **was** built ten years ago.
Why **do** you want to go home?
lesson.note: have / can't / was / do are auxiliary (= helping) verbs.

lesson.heading: Not repeating the main verb
lesson.text: You can use an auxiliary verb on its own when you don't want to repeat something. We use **do/does/did** for the present and past simple.

examples.text: Jessica could lend me the money, but **she won't**.
examples.note: = she won't lend me the money

examples.text: 'Does Simon live in London?' '**He did**, but **he doesn't** any more.'

lesson.heading: Denying what somebody says
lesson.text: You can also use auxiliary verbs to deny what somebody says (= to say it is not true).

examples.note: = I'm not sitting in your place

examples.text: 'You didn't lock the door before you left.' 'Yes, **I did**.'

lesson.heading: Have you? Isn't she? Did it?
lesson.text: We use **have you? / isn't she? / are they?** etc. to show that we are interested in what somebody has said, or to show surprise.

examples.text: 'I've just seen Steven.' 'Oh, **have you**? How is he?'
'Lisa isn't very well today.' '**Isn't she**? What's wrong with her?'
'It rained every day during our holiday.' '**Did it**? What a shame!'
'James and Tanya are getting married.' '**Are they**? Really?'

lesson.heading: So am I / Neither do I
lesson.text: We use auxiliary verbs with **so** and **neither**. Note the word order: the verb comes before the subject. Instead of neither, you can use **nor** or **not ... either**.

examples.text: Sarah can't drive and **neither can Mark**.
I passed the exam and **so did Paul**.
'I don't know.' '**Neither do I**.' or '**Nor do I**.' or '**I don't either**.'

lesson.heading: I think so / I suppose so
lesson.text: You can say **I think so / I suppose so** etc. when you don't want to repeat something. In the same way we say **I hope so, I expect so, I guess so** and **I'm afraid so**.

examples.note: = I suppose she is working tomorrow

examples.text: 'Will you be at home this evening?' '**I expect so**.'
examples.note: = I expect I'll be at home this evening

lesson.heading: The negative forms
rows: I think so / I expect so
I **don't think so** / I **don't expect so**
I hope so / I'm afraid so
I guess so / I suppose so
lesson.note: 'Do you think it will rain?' 'I hope so. / I hope not.' (not I don't hope so)

lesson.text: Match the auxiliary to the tense of the other speaker: *I've seen ...* - *Have you?*; *It rained ...* - *Did it?*; *I'm tired* - *So am I*.

exercises.prompt: I like hot weather, but Ann ___.
exercises.explanation: Present simple, so use does; Ann does not like it: Ann doesn't.

exercises.prompt: 'Is Andy here?' 'He ___ five minutes ago, but I think he's gone home now.'
exercises.explanation: He was here five minutes ago - the past of is, so the auxiliary is was.

exercises.prompt: I haven't travelled much, but Gary ___.
exercises.explanation: Gary has travelled a lot - the present perfect auxiliary is has.

exercises.prompt: Amy says: 'I like football.' You never agree with Amy. What do you say?
exercises.explanation: I like is present simple, so the auxiliary is do: Do you? I don't.

exercises.prompt: Amy says: 'I didn't enjoy the film.' You never agree with Amy. What do you say?
exercises.explanation: didn't enjoy is past simple, so the auxiliary is did: Didn't you? I did.

exercises.prompt: Tina tells you something and the same is true for you. Match each statement with your reply using So ... or Neither ... .

pairs.left: I won't be at home tomorrow.
I'd like to live somewhere else.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order. Sarah and Mark both have no driving licence.
exercises.answer: Sarah can't drive and neither can Mark.
exercises.explanation: After neither the verb comes before the subject: neither can Mark.

exercises.statement: I passed the exam and so Paul did.
exercises.explanation: I passed the exam and so did Paul. After so and neither the verb comes before the subject.

exercises.prompt: You need more money. Sam asks: 'Do you think you'll get a pay rise?' You answer: '___.'
exercises.explanation: You want it to happen, so: I hope so (= I hope I'll get a pay rise).

exercises.prompt: You're going to a party. You can't stand John. Sam asks: 'Will John be at the party?' You answer: '___.'
exercises.explanation: The negative of I hope so is I hope not (not I don't hope so).

exercises.prompt: You're not sure whether Amy is married, but she probably isn't. Sam asks: 'Is Amy married?' You answer: '___.'
exercises.explanation: The negative of I think so is I don't think so.

exercises.prompt: You are the receptionist at a hotel. The hotel is full. Sam asks: 'Do you have a room for tonight?' What do you say?
exercises.explanation: The negative of I'm afraid so is I'm afraid not.
